title: Ecology Basics
summary: In this lesson students will learn what ecosystems are, how organisms are linked through food webs, and how energy moves through these systems. They will also explore the major types of biomes and their characteristics.
objectives: Define ecosystem, food web, energy flow, and biome
Explain how energy is transferred through trophic levels
Identify and compare at least three major biomes
Create a simple food web diagram for a given ecosystem
prerequisites: Students should already understand basic cell structure, metabolism, and the concept of organisms from earlier lessons.
why: Understanding ecosystems helps us see how all living things depend on each other, which is essential for protecting the environment and managing natural resources.
Knowledge of biomes and energy flow informs real‑world issues such as climate change, conservation, and sustainable agriculture.

sections.heading: What Is an Ecosystem?
sections.body:
An **ecosystem** is simply a group of living things—plants, animals, fungi, and tiny microbes—living together in one place and interacting with the non‑living parts around them, such as water, soil, rocks, and sunlight. Think of it as a neighborhood where every resident (the living organisms) depends on the streets, houses, and utilities (the physical environment) to survive, and at the same time each resident changes the neighborhood in some way.

> **Definition:** An ecosystem is a community of living organisms plus the physical environment they share, all linked by the flow of energy and the cycling of matter.

Why do we talk about ecosystems?  By grouping organisms and their surroundings together, scientists can see patterns that are invisible when looking at a single species. For example, if a pond loses its algae because of pollution, the fish that eat the algae will also decline, and the insects that feed on the fish may disappear too. Understanding the whole system helps us predict what will happen when one part changes.

**Every word matters the first time it appears.**  
- *Community* means all the different species that live together in the same place.  
- *Physical environment* includes everything that is not alive: water, air, soil, temperature, and light.  
- *Interaction* refers to any way the living things affect each other or the environment, such as eating, sheltering, or changing the chemistry of the water.

A concrete example helps. Imagine a small forest pond:

1. **Living parts** – tiny algae float on the surface, water insects swim beneath, tadpoles eat the insects, and a frog sits on a lily pad waiting for a meal.  
2. **Non‑living parts** – the water itself, the sunlight that fuels photosynthesis, the oxygen dissolved in the water, and the muddy bottom that provides nutrients.  

All these pieces are linked. Sunlight lets algae grow; algae produce oxygen and food; insects eat algae; tadpoles eat insects; frogs eat tadpoles. When the pond freezes in winter, the whole process slows down, showing how temperature (a physical factor) controls the activity of the community.

> **In daily life:** A backyard garden is a tiny ecosystem. The soil, water, sunlight, worms, insects, and the vegetables you grow all interact. If you stop watering, the plants wilt, the insects lose food, and the worms die, showing the chain of effects.

Another example is a forest. Trees capture sunlight and turn carbon dioxide into wood and leaves. Deer browse the leaves, wolves hunt the deer, and fungi break down fallen logs, returning nutrients to the soil for new trees. The forest’s climate, the amount of rain, and the type of soil are all part of its physical environment.

When we study ecosystems, we often look at two big flows:

- **Energy flow** – energy enters as sunlight, moves through producers (plants) to consumers (herbivores, carnivores), and finally leaves as heat.  
- **Matter cycling** – elements like carbon, nitrogen, and water move in a loop: plants take up carbon dioxide, animals release carbon dioxide when they breathe, and decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead material, returning nutrients to the soil.

These flows can be written simply as:

$$\text{Energy}_{\text{sun}} \rightarrow \text{Producers} \rightarrow \text{Consumers} \rightarrow \text{Heat}$$

> **Note:** Energy always moves in one direction (from sun to heat), while matter recycles continuously within the ecosystem.

Understanding ecosystems is useful because it shows us how human actions—like cutting down trees, polluting a river, or adding fertilizers—can ripple through the whole system. By seeing the connections, we can make better choices to keep ecosystems healthy.

> **Common mistake:** Thinking of a species in isolation. A single animal does not exist alone; its survival depends on the whole network of plants, other animals, and the environment around it.

Remember that an ecosystem is not just a collection of species, but a dynamic web of relationships that includes both living and non‑living parts. When any piece changes, the whole web feels the effect. This perspective is the foundation for everything we will study next—food chains, energy flow, biomes, and the impact of humans on the natural world.

sections.heading: Components of an Ecosystem
sections.body:
Components of an ecosystem are the living parts and the non‑living parts that interact all the time.  
The living parts are called **biotic** factors; the non‑living parts are called **abiotic** factors.  
Understanding how these two groups affect each other helps us see why a pond can stay clear, why a desert is dry, and why a forest can recover after a fire.

**Biotic factors** are any organisms you can see or touch: plants, animals, fungi, and the countless microbes (bacteria and tiny fungi) that live in soil, water, and even on our skin.  
- **Plants** make their own food using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide.  
- **Animals** eat plants or other animals to obtain energy.  
- **Microbes** break down dead material, turning it back into nutrients that plants can use again.

**Abiotic factors** are the physical and chemical elements of the environment that do not grow or reproduce. The most important ones are:

- **Water** – supplies the medium for chemical reactions and transports nutrients.  
- **Sunlight** – provides the energy that plants capture through photosynthesis.  
- **Soil** – a mixture of mineral particles, organic matter, air, and water that holds nutrients and anchors plant roots.  
- **Temperature**, **air (oxygen, carbon dioxide)**, and **pH** (a measure of acidity) also belong to this group.

> **Definition:** *Biotic* = living components of an ecosystem; *Abiotic* = non‑living components.

### How biotic and abiotic factors influence each other

1. **Sunlight → Plant growth**  
   Sunlight hits a leaf, and the plant uses it to turn carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the air and water (H₂O) from the soil into sugars. This process is called *photosynthesis* and can be written simply as  

   $$6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2$$  

   The sugar is the plant’s food, and the oxygen (O₂) is released into the air for animals to breathe.

2. **Plants → Soil quality**  
   Plant roots dig into the soil, breaking up rocks and creating channels for water to flow. When leaves fall and decompose, microbes break them down, adding organic matter to the soil. This improves the soil’s ability to hold water and nutrients, which in turn helps more plants grow.

3. **Animals → Water cycle**  
   When an animal drinks water and later excretes waste, it returns nutrients to the soil and water bodies. Some animals, like beavers, build dams that change water flow, creating new wet habitats for other species.

4. **Microbes → Nutrient recycling**  
   After a leaf dies, microbes decompose it, releasing nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and other elements back into the soil. These nutrients are essential for new plant growth. Without microbes, dead material would pile up and nutrients would become locked away.

5. **Temperature → Metabolic rates**  
   Most biochemical reactions happen faster at warmer temperatures. In a cold lake, fish move slowly because their metabolism is slowed. In a warm pond, algae can multiply quickly, sometimes causing harmful “blooms” that reduce oxygen for other organisms.

> **In daily life:** Think of a kitchen garden. The sun (abiotic) lets the tomatoes grow (biotic). The tomatoes drop leaves that decompose, enriching the soil (abiotic) for the next planting season.

### Feedback loops

Ecosystems often contain *feedback loops*, where a change in one factor triggers a chain of reactions that eventually influences the original factor. For example, more plants increase soil organic matter, which holds more water, which allows even more plants to thrive. Conversely, if a drought dries the soil, plants die, microbes have less food, nutrient recycling slows, and the ecosystem becomes less productive.

> **Remember:** Every living thing depends on at least three abiotic factors—water, sunlight, and soil nutrients—to survive, and every abiotic factor is altered by the living things around it.

### Why this matters

Recognizing the two‑part nature of ecosystems helps us predict what will happen when we change one part. If we remove a predator (a biotic factor), prey populations may explode, over‑eating plants and depleting soil nutrients. If we pollute a river (an abiotic factor), fish and the microbes that clean the water can die, affecting the whole food web.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that “living” and “non‑living” parts act independently. In reality, they are tightly linked; a change in one almost always changes the other.

sections.heading: Food Chains and Food Webs
sections.body:
Imagine a tiny garden where a blade of grass catches sunlight, a rabbit nibbles the grass, and a hawk swoops down to catch the rabbit. This straight line of who‑eats‑who is called a **food chain**.  

> **Definition:** *Food chain* – a simple, linear sequence that shows how energy moves from a plant (producer) to an animal that eats the plant (primary consumer), then to an animal that eats that consumer (secondary consumer), and so on.

Why do we care about food chains? They let us see the direction of energy flow in nature. Energy always moves **one way** – from the sun to plants, then to animals – and never loops back in the same form. Knowing the chain helps us predict what might happen if one link disappears.  

**Step 1: Producers** – The first link is always a *producer*, a plant or algae that can make its own food using sunlight through a process called **photosynthesis**. In photosynthesis, plants turn light energy into chemical energy stored in sugars. The basic equation is  

$$
6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{light energy} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2
$$  

**Step 2: Primary consumers** – Animals that eat only producers are *primary consumers* (herbivores). A grasshopper that munches on grass is a primary consumer.  

**Step 3: Secondary and tertiary consumers** – Animals that eat herbivores are *secondary consumers* (carnivores or omnivores). A frog that eats the grasshopper is a secondary consumer. If a snake then eats the frog, the snake is a *tertiary consumer*.  

> **Note:** Only about **10 %** of the energy stored in one level is passed to the next level. The rest is used for metabolism, heat, or lost as waste. This is called the **10 % rule**.

Because each step loses most of its energy, food chains are usually short—often only three or four links long.  

### From Chains to Webs  

In a real garden, many animals eat many different foods. The rabbit might also eat clover, and the hawk might catch a mouse as well as a rabbit. When we draw all the possible connections, we get a **food web**.  

> **In daily life:** Think of a social network. One person (the producer) posts a photo, several friends (primary consumers) share it, and then their friends (secondary consumers) comment and repost. The information spreads through many overlapping paths, just like energy spreads through a food web.

A food web shows that ecosystems are **interconnected**. If one species declines, several other links are affected. For example, if a disease wipes out many grasshoppers, frogs lose a major food source, and snakes may have to rely more on mice.  

### Building a Simple Web  

1. **List the producers** – grass, algae, small trees.  
2. **Add primary consumers** – insects, rabbits, zooplankton.  
3. **Add secondary consumers** – frogs, small fish, deer.  
4. **Add tertiary consumers** – hawks, larger fish, wolves.  

Draw arrows from each animal to the food it eats. Where arrows cross, you have a web.  

> **Common mistake:** Drawing a “circular” food chain where a predator eventually eats the original producer. Energy cannot flow in a circle; it always moves outward from the sun.  

### Why Food Webs Matter  

Understanding webs helps ecologists predict the impact of human activities. If we overfish a small fish that many larger fish rely on, the whole web can collapse, leading to fewer predators and an overabundance of the fish’s prey (often algae that can cause harmful blooms).  

**Remember:** Energy starts with the sun, is captured by producers, and moves up through consumers, losing about 90 % at each step. Food webs illustrate the many pathways this energy can travel, showing the delicate balance that keeps ecosystems healthy.

sections.heading: Energy Flow and Trophic Levels
sections.body:
Energy moves through an ecosystem in a step‑by‑step ladder called **trophic levels**.  
The first level is made up of **producers** – plants, algae and some bacteria that can turn sunlight into chemical energy through photosynthesis.  
The next level contains **herbivores**, animals that eat only producers.  
Above them are **carnivores**, which eat other animals, and **omnivores**, which eat both plants and animals.  
At the bottom, or rather the side, are **decomposers** – fungi and bacteria that break down dead material and waste, returning nutrients to the soil.

> **Definition:** *Trophic level* – a group of organisms that share the same position in a food chain, receiving energy from the level directly below them.

Why does only a small fraction of energy move upward? When a plant captures sunlight, it stores that energy in the form of sugars. When an herbivore eats the plant, the herbivore must use part of those sugars for its own breathing, movement, growth and heat loss. The rest is stored in its body tissue and can be passed to the next consumer. However, each step wastes energy as heat, according to the **second law of thermodynamics**: energy transformations are never 100 % efficient.

The classic rule is that **about 10 % of the energy** in one trophic level is transferred to the next. This is called the **10 % rule**.

$$
\text{Energy}_{\text{next level}} \approx 0.10 \times \text{Energy}_{\text{current level}}
$$

If a grassland produces 10 000 kcal of energy in a year, only about 1 000 kcal will be available to the herbivores that eat the grass. Those herbivores will pass roughly 100 kcal to the carnivores that eat them, and so on. The rest is lost as heat, used for metabolism, or left behind in waste that decomposers later recycle.

> **In daily life:** Think of a light bulb that is only 10 % efficient. Most of the electricity you plug in is turned into heat, not light. In the same way, most energy in an ecosystem ends up as heat, not as food for the next level.

Understanding this energy loss explains why food chains are usually short. A typical chain has only three or four trophic levels before there isn’t enough energy left to support another level of large predators. This also shows why **apex predators** (top‑level carnivores) are relatively rare and need large territories to find enough food.

Decomposers play a special role. They do not fit neatly into the upward ladder because they obtain energy from dead organic matter rather than from living prey. By breaking down dead plants, animals and waste, they release nutrients back into the soil, allowing producers to grow again. In doing so, they close the loop of matter, even though the energy they use still follows the 10 % rule when they are eaten by scavengers.

> **Note:** Energy flow is one‑way (upward), but matter (like carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus) cycles continuously through all trophic levels, thanks to decomposers.

A common mistake is to think that a predator gets all the energy from the prey it eats. In reality, the predator only captures a fraction of the prey’s stored energy, and most of that fraction is again lost as heat when the predator lives and moves.

> **Remember:** Only about **10 %** of the energy at one trophic level is passed to the next. This limits the length of food chains and makes producers the most important source of energy in any ecosystem.

sections.heading: Biomes: Large‑Scale Ecosystems
sections.body:
A **biome** is a huge area of the Earth that shares a similar climate, plants, and animals.  
Think of a biome as a “neighborhood” for living things that is defined mainly by how much heat and water it gets.  
Because temperature and moisture control which plants can grow, they also decide which animals can live there.  

> **Definition:** A biome is a large‑scale ecosystem whose characteristic plants and animals are shaped by the region’s climate (temperature and precipitation) and the amount of solar energy it receives.

---

### How climate shapes a biome  

1. **Temperature** tells us how warm or cold a place is on average.  
2. **Precipitation** tells us how much water falls as rain or snow each year.  

When we combine these two numbers we can predict what kind of vegetation will dominate, and that vegetation forms the “base” of the food web.  

For example, a place that is warm **and** gets a lot of rain can support tall, broad‑leaf trees that need lots of water and sunlight. A place that is cold **and** dry can only support low‑lying plants that can survive freezing temperatures.

---

### Three classic biomes  

| Biome | Typical Climate (°C / mm yr⁻¹) | Dominant Plants | Typical Animals | Why the plants and animals fit |
|-------|------------------------------|----------------|----------------|------------------------------|
| **Tropical Rainforest** | 20‑30 °C, > 2000 mm | Tall evergreen trees, vines, epiphytes (plants that grow on other plants) | Jaguars, toucans, insects, many primates | Warm year‑round and abundant rain give plants enough energy to grow very tall. The dense canopy creates many layers, each offering a different habitat for animals. |
| **Desert** | 10‑40 °C (day), < 5 °C (night), < 250 mm | Succulents, drought‑tolerant shrubs, sparse grasses | Camels, fennec foxes, side‑winder snakes, beetles | Very little rain means water is scarce, so plants store water (succulents) or have deep roots. Animals are often nocturnal to avoid daytime heat and obtain water from food. |
| **Tundra** | –30 °C to 10 °C, < 250 mm | Mosses, lichens, dwarf shrubs, low grasses | Caribou, Arctic foxes, snowy owls, lemmings | Cold temperatures limit plant growth to short, low‑lying species that can survive a short growing season. Animals have thick fur or feathers and often migrate to find food. |

#### Why these differences matter  

- **Energy availability**: Sunlight is the ultimate energy source. In the rainforest, sunlight reaches the forest floor because the canopy is constantly refreshed by fast‑growing trees. In the desert, intense sunlight evaporates water quickly, so plants must conserve energy by growing slowly. In the tundra, low sun angles and long winters mean less energy reaches the ground, limiting plant growth.  

- **Water as a limiting factor**: Water acts like a “currency” that plants need to turn solar energy into biomass. When water is abundant (rainforest), plants can use most of the solar energy they receive, leading to high productivity. When water is scarce (desert) or frozen (tundra), productivity drops dramatically.  

> **Note:** Productivity = amount of biomass produced per unit area per year. It is highest in tropical rainforests and lowest in deserts and tundras because of differences in water and temperature.

---

### Everyday comparison  

Imagine three kitchens:

1. **Rainforest kitchen** – a well‑stocked pantry (plenty of water) and a strong stove (lots of sunlight). You can cook many dishes (many plant species) quickly.  
2. **Desert kitchen** – a tiny pantry (little water) and a very hot oven that burns food fast. You must cook slowly and use ingredients that last (succulents).  
3. **Tundra kitchen** – a cold kitchen with a weak stove (short daylight). You can only make simple, quick meals (mosses and lichens).  

Just as the kitchen’s resources limit what you can prepare, a biome’s climate limits what life can thrive there.

---

### Linking back to ecology  

Understanding biomes helps ecologists predict how changes in climate—like global warming—might shift the boundaries of these large‑scale ecosystems. If a desert receives more rain, it could start to support shrubs and eventually become a grassland. If a tundra warms, trees might move northward, turning it into a boreal forest.  

> **Remember:** A biome is defined by climate (temperature + precipitation) and the amount of solar energy that can be turned into plant growth. The plants set the stage for the animals that live there.

sections.heading: Human Impacts on Ecosystems
sections.body:
Human activities such as cutting down forests, dumping waste, and warming the planet change the way energy moves through nature and can even shift whole biomes – the large‑scale ecosystems that cover continents.

First, think of an ecosystem as a kitchen. The sun is the main power source, like a stove that heats food. Plants are the cooks that turn sunlight into chemical energy through photosynthesis. Animals then eat the plants, and the energy moves from one “dish” to the next. If the kitchen is clean and all the tools work, the meals are prepared smoothly. When we start removing tools or spilling chemicals, the cooking process gets messed up. In nature, the “tools” are trees, clean water, and stable climate; the “spills” are deforestation, pollution, and climate change.

**Deforestation** means cutting down large areas of forest. Trees are the biggest “energy collectors” on land because they have a huge leaf surface to capture sunlight. When we remove them, we reduce the total amount of solar energy that can be turned into food for the whole food chain. A simple way to see this is with the energy‑transfer rule that only about 10 % of the energy at one trophic level (the level of producers, primary consumers, etc.) passes to the next level.  

$$
E_{next}=0.10 \times E_{current}
$$  

If the original forest produced $E_{current}=1000$ kJ of energy per day, the herbivores would receive only $100$ kJ. After deforestation, the plant community might only produce $400$ kJ, so herbivores get $40$ kJ – a 60 % drop in food availability. This shortage can cause herbivore populations to shrink, which then reduces food for predators, rippling through the whole ecosystem.

**Pollution** adds unwanted chemicals or waste to air, water, or soil. Imagine sprinkling salt into a soup that is meant to be sweet. The taste changes, and some ingredients may become unusable. In a lake, excess nutrients from fertilizer runoff act like that salt: they cause algal blooms that block sunlight from reaching underwater plants. Those plants cannot photosynthesize, so the base of the aquatic food web weakens. Moreover, some pollutants are toxic and can kill organisms directly, removing links in the food chain.

**Climate change** is the gradual warming of the Earth caused mainly by burning fossil fuels, which releases carbon dioxide (CO₂) and other greenhouse gases. Warmer temperatures shift the “comfort zones” of many species, much like a person moving to a cooler room when it gets too hot. Some plants and animals can move to higher latitudes or higher elevations where the climate is still suitable. When many species move at the same time, the composition of a biome can change. For example, a temperate forest may gradually become more like a boreal forest if colder‑adapted trees replace the original species. This reshuffling also alters the pathways of energy flow because different species have different efficiencies in converting and passing on energy.

> **Note:** The 10 % energy‑transfer rule is an average; real ecosystems may have slightly more or less depending on the species involved.

> **In daily life:** When you see a clear‑cut hillside, think of it as a kitchen where the stove has been turned off – less food can be made, and the whole “meal” for wildlife shrinks.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that all energy lost by humans (e.g., from cars) disappears completely. In fact, most of it becomes heat, which still influences climate and therefore ecosystem energy balance.

> **Remember:** Small changes in one part of an ecosystem can cause big changes elsewhere because energy must move step by step through every trophic level. Keeping forests intact, reducing waste, and limiting greenhouse‑gas emissions help maintain the natural flow of energy and the stability of biomes.

sections.heading: Review and Application Activity
sections.body:
Imagine you are an artist who wants to draw a picture of a place where living things and non‑living things interact.  
Your picture will be a **diagram** – a simple drawing that shows how the parts of an ecosystem fit together.  
In this activity you will choose any ecosystem you like (a pond, a desert, a city park, a coral reef, etc.) and create a labeled diagram that includes three things:

1. **Abiotic factors** – the non‑living parts such as sunlight, temperature, water, soil, and wind.  
2. **Food web** – the network of who eats whom, starting with producers and moving up through herbivores, carnivores, and decomposers.  
3. **Biome** – the large‑scale classification that tells us what kind of ecosystem it is (e.g., forest, grassland, tundra).

Below is a step‑by‑step guide that walks you through the process, explaining every new word the first time it appears.

---

> **Definition:** *Ecosystem* – a community of living organisms (plants, animals, microbes) interacting with the non‑living environment (air, water, minerals) in a particular area.

### Step 1: Pick Your Ecosystem

Think of a place you have visited or can imagine clearly. It could be:

- The backyard garden where you see flowers, insects, and soil.  
- A local lake with fish, reeds, and sunlight.  
- A classroom terrarium you have built.  

Choosing something familiar makes it easier to notice details and label them correctly.

### Step 2: List the Abiotic Factors

Write down at least **four** abiotic factors that are important for your chosen ecosystem.  
Examples:

- **Sunlight** – provides energy for photosynthesis.  
- **Water** – needed for plants and animals to survive.  
- **Temperature** – influences which species can live there.  
- **Soil type** – determines which plants can grow.

If you are drawing a pond, you might also include **pH** (how acidic or basic the water is) and **oxygen levels** in the water.

### Step 3: Identify the Main Living Groups

Divide the living organisms you know into three groups:

1. **Producers** – plants or algae that make their own food using sunlight (photosynthesis).  
2. **Consumers** – animals that eat other organisms. They can be **herbivores** (eat plants), **carnivores** (eat meat), or **omnivores** (eat both).  
3. **Decomposers** – bacteria and fungi that break down dead material, returning nutrients to the soil or water.

Write down at least two examples for each group. For a forest, producers could be oak trees and ferns; herbivores might be deer and caterpillars; carnivores could be wolves and hawks; decomposers include mushroom fungi and soil bacteria.

### Step 4: Build a Simple Food Web

Start with the producers at the bottom. Draw arrows from each producer to the consumers that eat it. Then draw arrows from those consumers to the next level of predators. Finally, add arrows from all dead plants and animals to the decomposers.

**Why arrows?**  
Arrows show the direction of energy flow – from the food source to the eater. Energy always moves **one way**; it never goes backward.

> **Note:** A **food chain** is a single line of who eats whom, while a **food web** shows many interconnected chains. Use a web because real ecosystems are complex.

### Step 5: Label the Biome

Look up the broad classification of your ecosystem. Biomes are large regions with similar climate, plants, and animals. Common biomes include:

- **Temperate forest** – moderate rainfall, deciduous trees.  
- **Grassland** – wide open spaces, grasses dominate, few trees.  
- **Desert** – very little rain, extreme temperature changes.  
- **Freshwater lake** – standing water, moderate temperature, diverse fish.

Write the biome name near the top of your diagram and maybe add a tiny icon (a leaf for forest, a cactus for desert) to help you remember.

### Step 6: Draw and Label

Now put everything on paper or a digital canvas:

1. Sketch the landscape (water, hills, trees).  
2. Place icons for abiotic factors around the edges (a sun for sunlight, a droplet for water, a thermometer for temperature).  
3. Draw the food web in the center, using arrows and labeling each organism.  
4. Write the biome name clearly at the top.

Make sure every part has a label. If you run out of space, use abbreviations like **P** for producer, **H** for herbivore, **C** for carnivore, **D** for decomposer, and include a legend.

### Step 7: Reflect on What You Learned

Answer these short questions on the back of your diagram:

- How does energy enter the ecosystem?  
- What would happen if one key producer disappeared?  
- Which abiotic factor seems most limiting for the organisms you listed?

Writing brief answers helps you see the connections you just drew.

> **In daily life:** Creating a diagram is like making a map of your kitchen. You list the appliances (abiotic), the foods you cook (producers), the people who eat them (consumers), and the trash that gets recycled (decomposers). The map helps you understand how everything works together.

### Final Checklist

- [ ] Chosen ecosystem is clearly named.  
- [ ] At least four abiotic factors are listed and labeled.  
- [ ] Producers, consumers, and decomposers are identified with examples.  
- [ ] Food web arrows show correct direction of energy flow.  
- [ ] Biome name is written and matched to the ecosystem.  
- [ ] All parts are labeled; a legend is included if needed.  

When you finish, you will have a visual summary that shows how living and non‑living parts interact, how energy moves, and where the ecosystem fits in the world’s larger patterns. This diagram will be a useful study tool for future lessons on ecology and for explaining ecosystems to friends and family.

practice.q: Define an ecosystem in one sentence.
practice.a: An ecosystem is a community of living organisms (plants, animals, microbes) interacting with each other and with the non‑living parts of their environment (air, water, soil, sunlight) as a single functional unit.

practice.q: What is the main difference between a food chain and a food web?
practice.a: A food chain shows a single, linear path of energy flow from a producer to successive consumers, while a food web shows many interconnected food chains, illustrating that most organisms eat and are eaten by multiple other species.

practice.q: Explain why energy decreases at each trophic level in an ecosystem.
practice.a: Energy decreases because only about 10 % of the energy stored in the biomass of one trophic level is transferred to the next level; the rest is lost as heat during metabolism, used for movement, growth, and reproduction, or excreted as waste. This loss limits the number of trophic levels an ecosystem can support.

practice.q: Compare the characteristics of a desert biome and a tropical rainforest biome.
practice.a: A desert biome has very low rainfall (often <250 mm per year), extreme temperature swings between day and night, sparse vegetation (cacti, shrubs), and animals adapted to conserve water. A tropical rainforest receives high rainfall (over 2000 mm per year), has warm temperatures year‑round, dense multi‑layered vegetation with high biodiversity, and animals adapted to a humid, stable climate.

practice.q: Apply the concept of energy flow to explain why a top predator, such as a tiger, needs a large territory compared to a primary consumer, such as a rabbit.
practice.a: A tiger occupies a higher trophic level and receives only about 10 % of the energy from the herbivores it eats. To obtain enough food, the tiger must hunt many rabbits, each of which has gathered energy from many plants. Because the energy available per unit area is low at the top level, the tiger must cover a larger area to encounter sufficient prey, whereas a rabbit, as a primary consumer, can meet its energy needs within a smaller area rich in vegetation.

practice.q: Human activity often fragments habitats. Describe how habitat fragmentation can alter food webs and give one specific example.
practice.a: Habitat fragmentation breaks a continuous ecosystem into isolated patches, reducing the size of populations and limiting movement of species. This can remove certain predators or prey from a local food web, simplifying the web and potentially causing overpopulation of some species and decline of others. For example, when forest patches are separated by roads, large predators like wolves may disappear, leading to an increase in deer numbers, which then overgraze vegetation and reduce plant diversity.

recap: An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with the non‑living environment, linked by energy flow and matter cycling. It consists of biotic (plants, animals, microbes) and abiotic (sunlight, water, soil) factors, organized into food chains, food webs, and trophic levels. Large‑scale ecosystems are called biomes, which are shaped mainly by temperature and precipitation. Human activities can disrupt these connections, affecting energy flow and ecosystem health.

key_terms.meaning: A community of living organisms plus the physical environment they share, linked by energy flow and matter cycling.
The living parts of an ecosystem, such as plants, animals, fungi, and microbes.
The non‑living parts of an ecosystem, such as sunlight, water, temperature, soil, and minerals.
A linear sequence showing who eats whom, illustrating the direction of energy flow from producers to consumers.
A group of organisms that occupy the same position in a food chain and obtain energy from the level below.
A large‑scale ecosystem defined by its climate, dominant vegetation, and characteristic animal life.
Organisms like fungi and bacteria that break down dead material, returning nutrients to the environment.
The large‑scale removal of forest trees, which reduces the ecosystem’s ability to capture solar energy and can alter climate.

quiz.q: What does the term 'biotic factor' refer to?
options: Living organisms such as plants and animals
quiz.why: Biotic factors are the living components of an ecosystem.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the first trophic level in most food chains?
quiz.why: Producers (plants, algae) capture solar energy and form the base of the food chain.

quiz.q: A desert and a tropical rainforest are examples of:
quiz.why: Both are large‑scale ecosystems defined by climate, called biomes.

quiz.q: Why does energy decrease as it moves up trophic levels?
options: Energy is lost as heat during metabolism
quiz.why: Only about 10% of energy is transferred; the rest is lost as heat.

quiz.q: Which process do producers use to make their own food?
quiz.why: Photosynthesis converts sunlight into chemical energy in plants and algae.

quiz.q: Deforestation most directly reduces which ecosystem function?
quiz.why: Trees are major producers that capture solar energy; removing them cuts that energy input.

flashcards.back: A community of living organisms plus the non‑living environment they share, linked by energy flow and matter cycling.
Any living component of an ecosystem (plants, animals, fungi, microbes).
Non‑living components such as sunlight, water, temperature, soil, and minerals.
A linear sequence that shows who eats whom, illustrating energy flow from producers to top consumers.
A group of organisms that occupy the same position in a food chain and receive energy from the level below.
A large‑scale ecosystem defined mainly by climate (temperature and precipitation) and its characteristic plants and animals.
Organisms like fungi and bacteria that break down dead material, recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem.
The large‑scale removal of forest trees, which reduces energy capture and can alter climate and habitats.
